title: How do you focus on what matters most in a case interview?
description: How to prioritise in a case interview so you spend time on the few factors that drive most of the answer, with examples and phrases.
hook: You focus on what matters most by asking, at every stage of the case, "which one or two things are most likely to explain the answer?", then sizing them and starting there. This is the 80/20 idea: in many problems a few causes explain most of the effect. You do not need it to be exactly 80/20; the habit of ranking by impact is what keeps you from running out of time in a 30-minute case.
body:
Where the idea comes from

The economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that about 80% of Italy's land was owned by about 20% of the people. Decades later the quality expert Joseph Juran turned the pattern into a management principle, which he called "the vital few and the useful many". The numbers vary from problem to problem, but the lesson holds: effort spread evenly is effort wasted.

What it looks like in practice

  • Two products make up most of the revenue, so a revenue drop is probably there.
  • Fuel and staff are a large share of an airline's costs, so a cost case starts there, not with stationery.
  • A handful of large customers may drive most of the profit in a business-to-business company.

How to use it

  1. When you lay out your structure, say which branch is likely to matter most, and why.
  2. When you get a breakdown, look for the biggest pieces and the biggest changes first.
  3. When you brainstorm, rank your ideas by impact and feasibility, then focus on the top two or three.

Prioritise by change, not just by size

Size alone can mislead you. Suppose a company's profit fell and two cost lines rose:

  • A $40M line rose 2%: an extra $800k.
  • A $2M line rose 50%: an extra $1M.

The smaller line explains more of the change. So the test is materiality × what has actually moved × relevance to the decision. In the same way, if two of ten product lines are 65% of sales, start there, but check whether one of the smaller lines carries most of the margin or fell the furthest. Quantify before you commit.

What it sounds like

Weak: "There are lots of possible causes. Let me go through each cost line in turn."
Strong: "There are several possible causes, but delivery is 40% of costs and was mentioned in the prompt, so I'd start there. I'll come back to the smaller lines if delivery doesn't explain the change."

A word of caution

Prioritising does not mean ignoring everything else. Show that your structure covers the whole problem, then say where you will start and why. Mention the smaller areas briefly and list them as next steps in your recommendation. Keep one alternative hypothesis alive in case the big branch turns out not to hold the answer.

Practise

1. An airline's costs rose $30M. Fuel ($400M) rose 5%, catering ($20M) rose 25%, airport fees ($150M) rose 3% and everything else added $0.5M. Where do you focus?

Show the answer

Fuel: $400M × 5% = $20M. Catering: $20M × 25% = $5M. Airport fees: $150M × 3% = $4.5M. Other: $0.5M. Total $30M. Fuel explains two-thirds, so start there, even though catering had the biggest percentage rise.

2. A B2B software company has 200 customers. The top 20 bring 70% of revenue. Profit fell. Where do you look first?

Show the answer

Start with the top 20: has any churned, downgraded or renegotiated price? But also ask for profit by customer, since large accounts often get big discounts and heavy support, so the profit problem could sit with them even if revenue held.

3. You have five minutes left and three possible growth ideas: one worth about $10M, one about $2M and one about $0.5M. How do you finish?

Show the answer

Recommend the $10M idea and give its main risk and next step. Mention the $2M idea as a follow-up and leave the $0.5M idea out unless it is almost free to do.

Where to practise next

Use the so-what habit to turn the biggest numbers into insights, and practise reading breakdowns quickly with waterfall charts and the chart drills.
